standard_text: Solve real-world and other mathematical problems involving rates and ratios using models and strategies such as reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.

progression.narrative: 6.RP.4 asks students to SOLVE problems with rates and ratios, and it names the tools: ratio tables, tape diagrams, double number lines, and equations. The logic runs from seeing to scaling to comparing. First a student has to scale one ratio -- multiply BOTH quantities by the same factor -- because every model in this standard is just a picture of that one move (S1). Rates are the special case where one quantity is 1: find the per-one amount and a table of totals falls out (S2). Then the standard's named models carry more weight: a table of equivalent ratios lets a student find a missing value even when the multiplier is large (S3), and an equation or expression makes the strategy portable -- divide the given amount by ITS ratio part, then multiply by the other part (S4). Unit rates then earn their keep in the real world: unit pricing and constant speed, where 'cheaper total' and 'cheaper per unit' are not the same thing (S5). Finally, the standard's ceiling: hold one quantity equal and compare two ratios at once, a genuinely multi-step problem (S6). Underneath it all sit two foundations: multiplication and division facts (the scaling engine) and the ability to read and write a ratio in the stated order.

steps.rationale: Every model the standard names -- table, tape diagram, double number line -- is a picture of one move: multiply both quantities in the ratio by the same factor. Students must own that move before any model can help them.

Rates are the ratio with a 1 in it. Finding the per-one amount and extending it ('$13 per hour, so 7 hours is 13 x 7') is the standard's simplest real-world demand and the root of unit pricing and constant speed.

The standard explicitly names 'reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios.' A table organizes the scaling move so a student can find a missing value even when the multiplier is big or the ratio is given in reverse order.

Equations are the standard's most portable model. Writing (given / its ratio part) x other part forces the student to attach each number to the right quantity -- the exact place reversed setups happen.

The standard's 'real-world problems' demand lands here: unit pricing and constant speed. A unit rate lets a student answer ANY 'how much for n' question and exposes that the lower total price is not always the better deal.

The standard's ceiling (Above Proficiency): compare two or more ratios by scaling each to a common quantity. This is multi-step -- two scalings plus a comparison -- and it breaks any student who compares raw ratio numbers directly.

skills.name: Recall multiplication and division facts used to scale ratios

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiply and divide single-digit numbers from memory

skills.i_do_script: Every ratio problem in this unit comes down to one multiplication or division fact -- like 32 divided by 4 is 8, then 7 times 8 is 56. If the facts are slow, the ratio thinking falls apart, so we practice them until they're automatic. If you don't know a fact, use one you DO know: 6 x 7 is 6 x 5 plus 6 x 2, so 30 + 12 = 42.

canonical_error.pattern: Cannot recall multiplication or division facts, so every ratio scaling step produces a wrong multiplier or wrong product
canonical_error.example: To scale 7:4 up to 32, the student needs 32 / 4 = 8 but says 6, then gets 7 x 6 = 42 instead of 56
canonical_error.why: Facts weren't automatized in grades 3-4. The student understands the scaling idea but can't execute it, so every answer downstream is unreliable.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- let's check that fact before we go on.
redirect_script.prompt: Say the fact family out loud: if 4 x 8 = 32, then 32 / 4 = 8. Write the triangle with 32 on top and 4 and 8 on the bottom, and read it both ways.
redirect_script.praise: You pulled that fact instantly -- that speed is what makes ratio scaling easy.

skills.item_template: A single multiplication or division fact, or a missing-factor equation. NR (numeric response). No context, no choices -- just the fact.

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 48 (confuses with 6x8), 36 (confuses with 6x6)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 28 (confuses with 7x4), 36 (confuses with 9x4)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 56 (confuses with 7x8), 48 (confuses with 8x6)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 54 (confuses with 6x9), 63 (confuses with 7x9)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 8 (confuses with 32/4), 6 (confuses with 36/6)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 8 (confuses with 40/5), 7 (confuses with 35/5)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 50 (confuses with 10x5), 65 (confuses with 13x5)

sample_items.distractor_logic: Common errors: 8 (confuses with 64/8), 7 (confuses with 56/8)

vocabulary.definition: A number you multiply. In 4 x 8 = 32, the factors are 4 and 8.
The answer to a multiplication problem. In 4 x 8 = 32, the product is 32.
The answer to a division problem. In 32 / 4 = 8, the quotient is 8.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to F2 (write ratios) or straight to S1 (scale a ratio) -- the facts are ready to support scaling.
next_steps.if_fail: Run short daily fact sprints on the 4s, 6s, 7s, and 8s families before pushing ratio work. Slow facts will sink every skill in this standard.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 32 / 4 = ?
Say it as a question about multiplication: 4 times WHAT makes 32?
If the student starts skip-counting from 4 on their fingers, that's fine for now -- but note it. The goal is recall, not counting.
You know 4 x 8 = 32. So what is 32 / 4? How are those two facts related?
Draw a fact triangle: 32 on top, 4 and 8 on the bottom corners.
Read the triangle three ways: 4 x 8 = 32, 32 / 4 = 8, 32 / 8 = 4. Which of those will ratio problems ask for most?
Division facts are just multiplication facts read backward. In ratio work you'll constantly ask '32 divided by 4' to find how many times a ratio was scaled up.
Quick sprint: 24 / 6? 7 x 6? 45 / 9? Answer as fast as you can.

printable_artifact.title: Fact Triangle Sprint
printable_artifact.instructions: For each fact triangle, write all three facts (one multiplication, two division). Time yourself -- try to beat your time on the second column.

skills.name: Write a ratio in the stated order from a real-world situation

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare two quantities using 'for every' language
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A bowl has 3 apples and 5 bananas. Finish the sentence: 'For every 3 apples there are ___ bananas.'

skills.i_do_script: A ratio compares two amounts IN ORDER. If a fruit bowl has 3 apples and 5 bananas, the ratio of apples to bananas is 3:5 -- apples were named first, so 3 comes first. The same bowl gives a different ratio, 5:3, if someone asks for bananas to apples. Order is the whole game.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the two numbers in the order they appear in the story instead of the order the question names them
canonical_error.example: 'A class has 12 boys and 14 girls. Write the ratio of girls to boys.' Student writes 12:14 because 12 appeared first in the sentence, instead of 14:12
canonical_error.why: The student matches numbers left-to-right from the story instead of matching each number to its named quantity. They haven't learned that the QUESTION's word order, not the story's, sets the ratio order.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- check the order before you write.
redirect_script.prompt: Underline the two quantity words in the question, in order. Then write each word down with its number under it. The first word's number goes first in the ratio.
redirect_script.praise: You matched each number to its word -- that's exactly how ratios stay in order.

skills.item_template: A one-sentence situation with two quantities. Student writes the ratio in the order the question names, using ':' notation. Mostly NR; a couple of MC items bait the reversed order and part-to-whole confusion.

sample_items.stem: A fruit bowl has 3 apples and 5 bananas. Write the ratio of apples to bananas.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversal risk: 5:3 if the student writes the bigger or later number first

sample_items.stem: A class has 12 boys and 14 girls. Write the ratio of girls to boys.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Canonical error: 12:14 -- student copies the story's number order instead of the question's word order

sample_items.stem: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of milk. Write the ratio of flour to milk.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversal risk: 3:2; 'for every' language must map to order

sample_items.stem: There are 4 red marbles and 7 blue marbles in a bag. Write the ratio of blue marbles to red marbles.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Canonical error: 4:7 -- red appears first in the story, but blue is named first in the question

sample_items.stem: A team won 9 games and lost 2 games. Write the ratio of wins to losses.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversal risk: 2:9; also part-to-whole risk 9:11 if student compares wins to all games

sample_items.stem: A parking lot has 6 trucks and 10 cars. Write the ratio of trucks to cars.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversal risk: 10:6; simplifying to 3:5 is also acceptable but not required

sample_items.stem: Which ratio compares 5 pencils to 8 pens?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 8:5 reverses the order; 5:13 and 13:8 compare a part to the whole (5 + 8 = 13) instead of part to part

sample_items.stem: A garden has 8 tulips and 3 roses. Write the ratio of roses to tulips.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Canonical error: 8:3 -- tulips appear first in the story, but roses are named first in the question

sample_items.stem: A jar has 4 red marbles and 6 green marbles. Which is the ratio of red marbles to ALL the marbles?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4:6 is part-to-part, not part-to-whole; 6:10 uses green instead of red; 10:4 reverses whole and part

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two amounts in a specific order, like 3:5 or '3 to 5.'
The phrase that signals a ratio: '2 cups of flour FOR EVERY 3 cups of milk' means the ratio 2:3.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S1: scale a ratio by multiplying both quantities. The student can read ratios -- now they learn to grow them.
next_steps.if_fail: Act ratios out with two colors of counters. Say the ratio sentence while pointing: '3 apples' (touch 3 red) 'for every 5 bananas' (touch 5 yellow). Repeat with the question order flipped.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'A class has 12 boys and 14 girls. Write the ratio of girls to boys.'
Read the QUESTION part out loud. Which quantity does it name first -- girls or boys?
Write the two words in the question's order with a blank under each: girls ___ , boys ___.
Now go back to the story. How many girls? How many boys? Fill in the blanks.
So what's the ratio of girls to boys?
If the student writes 12:14, they copied the story's number order. Don't correct -- point at the word 'girls' in the question and ask, 'Which number belongs to this word?'
Tricky check: is 12:14 the ratio of girls to boys, or of boys to girls? How do you know?
The question's word order is the boss. Match each number to its word, and the ratio writes itself.

printable_artifact.title: Ratio Order Match
printable_artifact.instructions: For each story, underline the two quantity words in the question, write each word with its number, then write the ratio in the question's order.

skills.name: Scale a ratio by multiplying both quantities by the same factor
skills.i_do_script: A ratio grows like a photo being enlarged: BOTH numbers get multiplied by the same factor. If flour to sugar is 2:3 and I use 8 cups of flour, I ask 'what did 2 get multiplied by to become 8?' That's 4 -- so sugar gets multiplied by 4 too: 3 x 4 = 12 cups. The trap is adding: 8 is 6 more than 2, but adding 6 to the sugar wrecks the recipe.

canonical_error.pattern: Uses additive reasoning -- adds the same amount to both quantities instead of multiplying both by the same factor
canonical_error.example: Ratio of flour to sugar is 2:3. Given 8 cups of flour, the student computes 8 - 2 = 6 and answers 3 + 6 = 9 cups of sugar instead of 3 x 4 = 12
canonical_error.why: The student sees 'the first number grew, so the second should grow by the same amount.' They're tracking the DIFFERENCE between the quantities instead of the multiplicative relationship, which is what keeps a ratio equivalent.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- did you add or multiply to get there?
redirect_script.prompt: Ask yourself: what did the first number get MULTIPLIED by? Write '2 x ? = 8' and solve it. Then multiply the second number by that same factor.
redirect_script.praise: You found the multiplier and used it on both numbers -- that's what keeps a ratio a ratio.

skills.item_template: A real-world ratio (both parts single-digit) plus a scaled amount of the first quantity (compatible numbers). Student finds the matching amount of the second quantity. MC with 4 choices baiting additive reasoning, or NR with a double number line.

sample_items.stem: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of sugar. If a baker uses 8 cups of flour, how many cups of sugar are needed?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9 adds the difference (8 - 2 = 6, then 3 + 6); 11 adds the sugar count to the flour count (8 + 3); 24 multiplies the given by the other ratio part (8 x 3)

sample_items.stem: The ratio of dogs to cats at a shelter is 3:4. If there are 15 dogs, how many cats are there?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 16 adds the difference (15 - 3 = 12, then 4 + 12); 12 uses the wrong multiplier (4 x 3); 60 multiplies the given by the other ratio part (15 x 4)

sample_items.stem: The double number line shows a cyclist's distance and time. How many miles does the cyclist ride in 4 hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who count ticks instead of reading values may answer 4; additive reasoners may answer 6 (3 + 3 once) instead of following the line to 12

sample_items.stem: A paint mix uses 5 drops of blue for every 2 drops of yellow. Mia uses 20 drops of blue. How many drops of yellow does she need?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 17 adds the difference (20 - 5 = 15, then 2 + 15); 10 multiplies the ratio parts (5 x 2); 40 multiplies the given by the other ratio part (20 x 2)

vocabulary.definition: Ratios that describe the same relationship, like 2:3 and 8:12. You get one from the other by multiplying both numbers by the same factor.
The factor both quantities get multiplied by. From 2:3 to 8:12 the multiplier is 4.
Two number lines lined up so matching pairs from a ratio sit at the same tick.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S2 (use a rate to find a total) or S3 (ratio tables) -- the scaling move is in place.
next_steps.if_fail: Check F2 first: can the student even write the ratio in order? If yes, rebuild scaling with counters -- physically make 2:3 three times and count what you get.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'Flour to sugar is 2:3. The baker uses 8 cups of flour. How much sugar?'
The flour went from 2 to 8. What happened to it -- what did 2 get multiplied by?
Write '2 x 4 = 8' and, under it, '3 x ? = ?'
If the flour was multiplied by 4, what has to happen to the sugar to keep the recipe tasting the same?
If the student says '8 is 6 more than 2, so sugar is 3 + 6 = 9,' don't correct yet -- have them build 2:3 with counters four times and count the sugar counters.
Count it: four groups of 3 sugar counters. How many? So is the answer 9 or 12?
Ratios scale by multiplying BOTH parts by the same factor. Adding the same amount to both breaks the recipe -- that's the number one trap in this whole unit.
Your turn: dogs to cats is 3:4 and there are 15 dogs. What's the multiplier, and how many cats?

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of stars to hearts in a pattern is 1:3. If you draw 4 stars, how many hearts do you draw?
The double number line shows a cookie recipe. How many cookies can you make with 6 cups of flour?
The ratio of red beads to blue beads on a bracelet is 3:5. If Ana uses 12 red beads, how many blue beads does she use?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier is 4. Watch for 14 (adds the difference 12 - 3 = 9 to the 5).

practice_problems.stem: Deshawn solved this ratio problem. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The ratio of pencils to erasers is 2:5.
practice_problems.answer: Deshawn added instead of multiplying. The pencils were MULTIPLIED by 4 (2 x 4 = 8), so the erasers are 5 x 4 = 20, not 11.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical additive-reasoning error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A smoothie uses 4 strawberries for every 6 blueberries. Marco uses 12 strawberries. How many blueberries does he need?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier is 3. Numbers share a factor -- watch for students multiplying 4 x 6 = 24.

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the missing number on the double number line.
practice_problems.notes: Dollars grow by 4 for every pound. The ? sits above 4 pounds: 4 x 4 = 16.

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of markers to crayons is 3:7. There are 21 crayons. How many markers are there?
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- the SECOND quantity is given. Multiplier is 21 / 7 = 3.

practice_problems.stem: Write your own word problem that uses the ratio 3:5 and has the answer 15. Then show the multiplier that solves it.
practice_problems.answer: Any problem scaling 3:5 by 3 and asking for the second quantity, e.g. 'Cats to dogs is 3:5. There are 9 cats. How many dogs?' Multiplier 3, so 5 x 3 = 15.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a problem shows the scaling relationship runs both directions.

activities.title: Multiplier Match-Up
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the ratio cards face up on the left and the answer cards on the right.
2. Partners take turns picking a ratio card, saying the multiplier OUT LOUD ('2 became 8, so times 4'), and matching it to its answer.
3. The partner checks by multiplying the second quantity by the stated multiplier.
4. Debrief: which card tempted you to add instead of multiply, and why?

activities.title: Build It in Batches
materials: Two colors of counters (about 40 of each)
activities.instructions:
1. Announce a ratio, e.g. 'red to yellow is 2:3.' Each student builds ONE batch on a plate: 2 red, 3 yellow.
2. Say: 'Build until you have 8 red total.' Students keep making full batches on new plates.
3. Ask: how many batches (plates)? How many yellow in all? Write it as 2:3 = 8:12.
4. Repeat with 3:4 up to 15 of the first color.
5. Debrief: could you add 6 to both numbers instead? Build 8 red and 9 yellow and check whether every plate still shows 2:3.

activities.title: Why Did Deshawn Add?
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Deshawn's work and let the group talk first.
2. Ask: what was Deshawn thinking? (His idea is sensible -- both numbers should grow.)
3. Have the group build the ratio with counters both ways -- multiplying and adding -- and check which one keeps every batch at 2:5.
4. Each student writes Deshawn a one-sentence tip.

content.worked_problem: Pencils to erasers is 2:5. There are 8 pencils. Deshawn wrote: 8 - 2 = 6, so 5 + 6 = 11 erasers.
content.error_step: Deshawn tracked how much the pencils GREW BY (+6) instead of what they were MULTIPLIED BY (x4).
content.why: Equivalent ratios come from multiplying both parts by the same factor. Adding the same amount to both parts changes the relationship -- 8:11 is not the same mix as 2:5, but 8:20 is.

strategy_links.why: Building ratio batches with counters makes 'multiply both parts' visible before it becomes an abstract rule.
The additive-reasoning error is predictable and analyzable -- dissecting a wrong 'add 6 to both' answer breaks the habit faster than more practice.
Whiteboard Pass shows instantly which students are multiplying and which are still adding on every single problem.

questioning_prompts: What did the first number get MULTIPLIED by? Prove it with a fact.
If we made this recipe in batches, how many batches is that?
You added 6 to both numbers. Does 8:9 taste the same as 2:3? How could we check?
Where would this pair sit on a double number line? Do the two values line up at the same tick?
Which number in the problem is the multiplier -- and which numbers are parts of the ratio?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the same amount to both quantities (8 - 2 = 6, so 3 + 6 = 9) instead of multiplying both by the same factor.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask yourself: what did the first number get MULTIPLIED by? Write '2 x ? = 8' and solve it. Then multiply the second number by that same factor.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the multiplier and used it on both numbers -- that's what keeps a ratio a ratio.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the two ratio numbers together (2 x 3 = 6) and offers that as the answer.
misconception_redirects.say: Those two numbers are PARTNERS in one ratio, not a multiplication problem. Circle the given amount in the story -- the multiplier connects the given amount to ITS ratio part.
misconception_redirects.praise: Now you're connecting the given number to its own ratio part before touching the other one.

quick_checks.prompt: Ratio 2:5, and the first quantity is now 10. What's the multiplier, and what's the second quantity?
quick_checks.look_for: Multiplier 5, answer 25, stated in that order. A student who answers 13 (5 + 8) is still reasoning additively; one who answers 10 is multiplying the ratio parts.

quick_checks.prompt: True or false: 4:6 and 8:10 are equivalent ratios.
quick_checks.look_for: False, because 4 was doubled but 6 wasn't (8:12 would be equivalent). 'True' means the student checked that both numbers grew, not that they grew by the same FACTOR.

worked_solution.stem: A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of sugar. If a baker uses 8 cups of flour, how many cups of sugar are needed?

steps.annotation: Find the multiplier: what did the flour get multiplied by to go from 2 to 8?
Multiply the sugar by the SAME factor. Both parts of a ratio scale together.
Divide both parts of 8:12 by 4 -- you get back 2:3, so the ratio held.

faded_example.stem: The ratio of dogs to cats at a shelter is 3:4. If there are 15 dogs, how many cats are there?

steps.annotation: The dogs went from 3 to 15 -- multiplied by 5.
Multiply the cats' ratio part by that same multiplier.
Check your pair: does your answer with 15 reduce back to 3:4?

sentence_starters: I multiplied both parts by ___, so the ratio stayed equivalent.

skills.name: Use a unit rate to find a total for any number of units
skills.i_do_script: A rate tells you the amount for ONE unit -- $12 per hour means every single hour earns $12. Once you know the per-one amount, any total is one multiplication away: 4 hours is 12 x 4 = $48. The trap comes when the problem gives a total instead of a rate: '$65 for 5 hours' is NOT $65 per hour -- you have to divide first (65 / 5 = $13 per hour) before you can scale.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats a total for several units as if it were the per-unit rate -- multiplies the total instead of finding the unit rate first
canonical_error.example: A babysitter is paid $65 for 5 hours. Asked about 7 hours, the student computes 65 x 7 = 455 instead of 65 / 5 = 13 per hour, then 13 x 7 = 91
canonical_error.why: The student sees a dollar amount next to 'per' or 'for' and assumes it is the rate for one unit. They haven't learned to ask 'is this amount for ONE, or for SEVERAL?' before multiplying.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- is that amount for ONE hour, or for FIVE?
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the amount and underline how many units it covers. If it covers more than one, divide first to get the for-ONE amount. Only then multiply.
redirect_script.praise: You checked 'for one or for several?' before multiplying -- that question saves you every time.

skills.item_template: A rate context (pay per hour, pages per minute, miles per gallon), often with a table of values that has one missing entry. Student extends the rate to a new number of units. NR, with an MC variant baiting the total-as-rate error.

sample_items.stem: A babysitter is paid $12 per hour. The table shows her pay. How much will she earn in 4 hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who lose track of the rate may add 12 to the last entry shown or miscount rows

sample_items.stem: Nora reads 8 pages every minute. The table shows her progress. How many pages will she read in 6 minutes?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students may continue the visible pattern one row at a time and slip (40), or add 8 + 6 = 14

sample_items.stem: A babysitter is paid $65 for 5 hours of babysitting. At this rate, how much would the babysitter make for 7 hours of babysitting?
sample_items.distractor_logic: $455 treats $65 as the per-hour rate (65 x 7); $78 adds one more hour's rate to the total ($65 + $13); $130 doubles the total instead of scaling by hours

sample_items.stem: A printer prints 30 pages in 5 minutes. At this rate, how many pages does it print in 9 minutes?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Total-as-rate error gives 30 x 9 = 270; unit rate is 30 / 5 = 6 pages per minute, then 6 x 9 = 54

vocabulary.definition: A ratio that compares two different kinds of units, like dollars and hours or miles and gallons.
The amount for exactly ONE unit -- $13 per hour, 8 pages per minute.
A signal word meaning 'for each one.' $12 per hour means every single hour earns $12.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S3 (ratio tables) or S5 (unit pricing and speed problems) -- the per-one idea is solid.
next_steps.if_fail: Check F1: are multiplication and division facts automatic? If yes, rebuild the per-one idea with a table -- fill in hours 1, 2, 3 one row at a time and ask what one hour is worth.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board: 'A babysitter is paid $65 for 5 hours. How much would she make for 7 hours?'
Is $65 what she earns for ONE hour, or for FIVE hours? How do you know?
If the student reaches for 65 x 7, stop and ask: 'If she made $65 EVERY hour, how much would 5 hours be? Does $325 match the story?' Let the contradiction do the correcting.
So how do we find what ONE hour is worth?
Write '65 / 5 = 13' and label it '$13 per hour.' Start a table: 1 hour -> 13, 2 hours -> 26.
Now that we know one hour is $13, what are 7 hours worth?
Sanity check: 7 hours should pay MORE than 5 hours but not seven times $65. Is $91 reasonable?
That two-step move -- divide to find the for-one amount, multiply to scale it -- is the engine behind every rate problem, unit price, and speed question in this standard.

practice_problems.stem: Apples cost $2 per pound. How much do 5 pounds cost?
A faucet fills 4 gallons every minute. Complete the table: how many gallons after 3 minutes?
Museum tickets cost $45 for 5 students. At this rate, how much do tickets cost for 8 students?
practice_problems.notes: Unit rate first: 45 / 5 = $9 per student, then 9 x 8. Watch for 45 x 8 = 360.

practice_problems.stem: Priya solved this rate problem. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: A dog walker earns $40 for 4 walks.
How much does she earn for 6 walks?
practice_problems.answer: Priya treated $40 as the pay for ONE walk, but it covers 4 walks. Unit rate: 40 / 4 = $10 per walk. Then 10 x 6 = $60.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical total-as-rate (per vs. total) error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A train travels 120 miles in 3 hours. At this rate, how far does it travel in 5 hours?
practice_problems.notes: Constant speed: 120 / 3 = 40 miles per hour, then 40 x 5.

practice_problems.stem: The table shows a photographer's fee. What does the photographer charge for 7 hours?
practice_problems.notes: Rate is hidden: 50 / 2 = $25 per hour, then 25 x 7. The table skips rows on purpose.

practice_problems.stem: Lemonade costs $3 per cup. Jamal spent $27. How many cups did he buy?
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction -- total given, units unknown. Divide instead of multiply.

practice_problems.stem: A babysitter earns $84 for 7 hours. What is her unit rate, and how would you find her pay for ANY number of hours? Explain in one sentence.
practice_problems.answer: $12 per hour (84 / 7). Multiply 12 by the number of hours.
practice_problems.notes: Explaining the general rule shows the student owns the per-one idea, not just one answer.

activities.title: For One or For Several?
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the story cards on the left and the unit-rate cards on the right.
2. For each story card, partners first say OUT LOUD whether the money amount is for ONE unit or for SEVERAL.
3. If it's for several, divide to find the unit rate, then match.
4. Debrief: which story tried to trick you into skipping the division?

activities.title: Rate Table Race
activities.instructions:
1. Write a rate on the board, e.g. '$7 per ticket.'
2. Call out a number of units ('9 tickets!'). Every student writes the total on their whiteboard and holds it up.
3. After three rounds, switch to a TOTAL clue ('$36 for 4 tickets -- now 6 tickets!') so students must divide first.
4. A team scores a point only if EVERY member's board is correct -- teammates check each other.
5. Debrief: what extra step showed up when the clue was a total instead of a rate?

activities.title: The $455 Babysitter
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show the group the flawed work and let them react before you say anything.
2. Ask: what did this student believe $65 meant?
3. Have the group compute what the babysitter would earn in 5 hours if $65 really were her hourly rate, and compare it to the story.
4. Each student writes the fixed solution and circles the division step.

content.worked_problem: A babysitter is paid $65 for 5 hours. For 7 hours: 65 x 7 = $455.
content.error_step: The student used $65 -- the pay for FIVE hours -- as if it were the pay for ONE hour.
content.why: An amount is only a unit rate if it covers exactly one unit. When it covers several, divide first: 65 / 5 = $13 per hour, then 13 x 7 = $91.

strategy_links.why: Short Number Talks on 'what is one worth?' ($48 for 4, 60 miles in 2 hours) make the divide-first move mental and automatic.
Thinking aloud the question 'is this amount for one or for several?' models the exact self-check that prevents the total-as-rate error.
The 65 x 7 error is common and diagnosable -- analyzing it directly teaches students to test whether an amount is really a per-one rate.

questioning_prompts: Is that amount for ONE unit or for SEVERAL? Point to the words that tell you.
What is one hour worth here? What is one pound worth?
Before you compute: should the answer be bigger or smaller than the amount in the story? Why?
Your table jumps from 3 hours to 7. Do you have to fill every row, or is there a faster way?
Where does the unit rate hide in your table -- which row shows it?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies a several-unit total as if it were a per-unit rate (65 x 7 for '$65 for 5 hours').
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the amount and underline how many units it covers. If it covers more than one, divide first to get the for-ONE amount. Only then multiply.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked 'for one or for several?' before multiplying -- that question saves you every time.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds the rate once instead of multiplying (12 + 4 = 16 for '$12 per hour, 4 hours').
misconception_redirects.say: Build the table one row at a time: 1 hour is 12, 2 hours is 24... is each row ADDING 12 once, or adding it for every hour? What operation does 'add 12 four times' become?
misconception_redirects.praise: Right -- repeated adding of the rate IS multiplication. You just found the shortcut.

quick_checks.prompt: $28 for 4 pounds of grapes. What is the unit price, and what do 6 pounds cost?
quick_checks.look_for: $7 per pound, $42. An answer of $168 (28 x 6) is the total-as-rate error; hesitation on 28 / 4 signals an F1 fact gap.

quick_checks.prompt: Point at the table row that shows the unit rate. (Show a table with rows 2->50, 4->100.)
quick_checks.look_for: Student says no row shows it and computes 1 -> 25. Pointing at the 2->50 row means they still equate 'first row' with 'unit rate.'

worked_solution.stem: A babysitter is paid $65 for 5 hours of babysitting. At this rate, how much would the babysitter make for 7 hours?

steps.annotation: First decide: is the amount for one unit or several? Here it covers 5 hours, so it is NOT the hourly rate.
Divide to find the for-ONE amount -- the unit rate.
Scale the unit rate by the new number of hours.
The unit rate rebuilds the original story, so it's right.

faded_example.stem: A train travels 120 miles in 3 hours. At this rate, how far does it travel in 5 hours?

steps.annotation: The 120 miles covers 3 hours, so divide to find the distance for ONE hour.
Multiply the unit rate by the new number of hours.
Check: does your unit rate times 3 give back 120?

sentence_starters: The amount is for ___ units, so first I divide to get the for-one amount.
The unit rate is ___ per ___, so ___ units is ___ x ___.

skills.name: Use a table of equivalent ratios to find a missing value
skills.i_do_script: A ratio table is rows of equivalent ratios -- every row is the original ratio multiplied by some factor. If daisies to roses is 7:4 and I need the row with 32 roses, I ask what 4 was multiplied by: 32 / 4 = 8. Then the daisies in that row are 7 x 8 = 56. The two numbers in one row are partners -- never multiply them together (7 x 4 = 28 answers nothing).

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the two numbers of the ratio together instead of finding the multiplier from the given quantity
canonical_error.example: Daisies to roses is 7:4 and there are 32 roses. Student answers 7 x 4 = 28 daisies instead of finding the multiplier 32 / 4 = 8 and computing 7 x 8 = 56
canonical_error.why: The student sees two numbers side by side and applies the most familiar move -- multiply them. They don't yet see the ratio pair as ONE relationship that the given quantity plugs into through a multiplier.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- those two numbers are partners, not a multiplication problem.
redirect_script.prompt: Put the given amount in the table under its OWN column. Now ask: what was that column's ratio number multiplied by to get there? Use that multiplier on the other column.
redirect_script.praise: You found the multiplier from the right column and carried it across -- that's exactly how ratio tables work.

skills.item_template: A real-world ratio (one part single-digit) shown as a table of equivalent ratios with a missing value in a later row. The multiplier is medium-large (4-10). MC with 4 choices or NR; the data_table figure is part of the item.

sample_items.stem: A flower shop creates bouquets of daisies and roses. The table shows the ratio of daisies to roses. How many daisies will be needed when 32 roses are used?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 28 multiplies the ratio numbers together (7 x 4); 49 uses the wrong multiplier (7 x 7); 25 subtracts (32 - 7)

sample_items.stem: A snack mix uses 3 cups of nuts for every 8 cups of cereal. The table shows the ratio. How many cups of nuts are needed for 40 cups of cereal?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 24 multiplies the ratio numbers together (3 x 8); 18 uses the wrong multiplier (3 x 6); 48 adds the cereal amounts (40 + 8)

sample_items.stem: A store sells 5 T-shirts for every 9 hats. The table shows the ratio. How many T-shirts are sold when 63 hats are sold?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 45 multiplies the ratio numbers together (5 x 9); 40 uses the wrong multiplier (5 x 8); 59 keeps the additive difference of 4 between the quantities (63 - 4)

sample_items.stem: A painter mixes 6 cups of white paint for every 2 cups of blue paint. The table shows the mix. How many cups of white paint go with 14 cups of blue paint?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Multiplying the ratio numbers gives 12; the multiplier is 14 / 2 = 7, so white = 6 x 7 = 42

vocabulary.definition: A table where every row shows the same ratio scaled by a different factor.
Ratios that describe the same relationship -- every row of a ratio table is equivalent to every other row.
The factor that connects the original ratio row to the row you need.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S4 (write the expression/equation) -- the table reasoning is ready to be compressed into symbols.
next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to S1 with small multipliers (2 and 3) and build the table row by row with counters before jumping rows.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the table on the board: Daisies 7, 14, 21, ? / Roses 4, 8, 12, 32. Say: 'The shop uses 7 daisies for every 4 roses.'
Look down the roses column: 4, 8, 12... then it jumps to 32. Which column does the given number 32 belong to, daisies or roses?
What was 4 multiplied by to become 32?
Write '4 x 8 = 32' next to the roses column, and draw an arrow carrying 'x 8' over to the daisies column.
So what do we do to 7 to fill the missing daisies?

If the student answers 28, they multiplied 7 x 4 -- the two ratio partners. Point at the table and ask: 'Is 28 daisies with 32 roses the same mix as 7 daisies with 4 roses? Check with the multiplier.'
Check the row 56 and 32: divide both by 8. Do you land back on 7 and 4?
In a ratio table, the move is always across-and-down with ONE multiplier -- never multiply the two partners in a row together.

practice_problems.stem: Complete the ratio table for 2:5. What number is missing?
The ratio of pencils to pens is 3:4. Complete the equivalent ratio: 9 pencils to ? pens.
A punch recipe uses 5 cups of juice for every 2 cups of soda. How many cups of juice are needed with 18 cups of soda?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier 18 / 2 = 9. Watch for 10 (5 x 2) -- the partners-multiplied error.

practice_problems.stem: Kira used a ratio table to solve this problem. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The ratio of daisies to roses is 6:4.
practice_problems.answer: Kira multiplied the two ratio numbers together -- it only LOOKED right because 6 x 4 happens to equal 24. The multiplier is 24 / 4 = 6, so daisies = 6 x 6 = 36.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the canonical partners-multiplied error. The coincidence (6 x 4 = 24) makes the wrong move feel confirmed.

practice_problems.stem: The table shows the ratio of granola bars to water bottles packed for a hike. How many granola bars go with 35 water bottles?
practice_problems.notes: The table skips rows: multiplier is 35 / 7 = 5, so 4 x 5 = 20.

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of laps to minutes for Ella's swim practice is 2:9. Ella swam 8 laps. How many minutes did she swim?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier 8 / 2 = 4, so 9 x 4 = 36. Watch for 18 (2 x 9).

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of roses to daisies is 4:7 -- careful, roses are named FIRST this time. How many roses are needed when 63 daisies are used?
practice_problems.notes: Reverse order (spec's 'difficult' move): the given 63 belongs to the SECOND quantity. Multiplier 63 / 7 = 9, so 4 x 9 = 36.

practice_problems.stem: Build your own ratio table for 3:5 with at least four rows, where the last row has 30 in the first column. Then explain how you found the last row.
practice_problems.answer: Rows such as 3:5, 6:10, 9:15, 30:50. Multiplier for the last row is 30 / 3 = 10, so the second column is 5 x 10 = 50.
practice_problems.notes: Producing a table shows the student can generate equivalent ratios, not just verify them.

activities.title: In the 2:3 Table or Not?
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out the headers 'Belongs in the 2:3 table' and 'Does NOT belong.'
2. Partners take turns drawing a card, stating the multiplier out loud if they think it belongs ('2 x 5 = 10 and 3 x 5 = 15 -- same multiplier'), and placing it.
3. The partner checks by dividing both numbers back down to see if they land on 2 and 3.
4. Debrief: what made 6:8 tempting, and what test caught it?

activities.title: The Lucky Wrong Answer
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Kira's work (6:4 ratio, 24 roses, answer '6 x 4 = 24 daisies') and ask the group whether her ANSWER or her METHOD is the problem.
2. Have the group test her method on a new row: with 8 roses, her method still gives 24 daisies -- does that make sense?
3. Rebuild the row correctly with a multiplier (24 / 4 = 6, then 6 x 6 = 36).
4. Debrief question: why is a method that 'got 24' still wrong?

content.worked_problem: Daisies to roses is 6:4. With 24 roses, Kira wrote 6 x 4 = 24 daisies.
content.error_step: Kira multiplied the two ratio partners together instead of finding what 4 was multiplied by to reach 24.
content.why: The two numbers in a ratio are one relationship, not a multiplication problem. Her method gives the same answer no matter how many roses there are -- the multiplier (24 / 4 = 6) is what connects the given amount to the answer, 6 x 6 = 36.

activities.title: Tape Diagram Bouquets
activities.instructions:
1. Students draw a tape diagram for daisies to roses 7:4 -- a bar of 7 boxes above a bar of 4 boxes.
2. Say: 'There are 32 roses. If 4 boxes hold 32 roses, how many roses per box?' Students write 8 inside every rose box.
3. Ask: 'Each daisy box holds the same amount. How many daisies in all?' Students write 8 in each of the 7 boxes and total them.
4. Repeat with 3:8 nuts to cereal and 40 cups of cereal.
5. Debrief: where does the multiplier live in the tape diagram? (Inside every box.)

strategy_links.why: Partners must verbalize the multiplier before placing a card or filling a row -- talking the 'x 8 across the row' move makes it a habit.
Tape diagrams and counter-built tables are the concrete and representational steps behind the abstract ratio table the test shows.
The partners-multiplied error (7 x 4 = 28) survives ordinary practice; analyzing a worked wrong answer -- especially a 'lucky' one -- kills it.

questioning_prompts: Which column does the given number belong to? Point to it before you compute anything.
What was that column's ratio number multiplied by? Prove it with a division.
You multiplied 7 by 4. What question does 7 x 4 answer in this story? Does anyone need that number?
Pick any two rows of the table. What multiplier connects them? Does it work for BOTH columns?
Could you solve this without writing every row? Which rows can you skip?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the two ratio numbers together (7 x 4 = 28) instead of finding the multiplier from the given quantity.
misconception_redirects.say: Put the given amount in the table under its OWN column. Now ask: what was that column's ratio number multiplied by to get there? Use that multiplier on the other column.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the multiplier from the right column and carried it across -- that's exactly how ratio tables work.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student puts the given number in the wrong column (treats 32 as daisies because daisies were named first).
misconception_redirects.say: Underline the unit next to the given number in the story -- 32 WHAT? Label both table columns, then place 32 under its unit before you do any math.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the number to its unit first -- now every step after that lands in the right column.

quick_checks.prompt: Ratio 3:8, and the second quantity is 40. What is the multiplier, and what is the first quantity?
quick_checks.look_for: Multiplier 5 (from 40 / 8), first quantity 15. An answer of 24 means the student multiplied the partners (3 x 8); 120 means they multiplied the given by the wrong part.

quick_checks.prompt: Show the row '10 and 14' from a table that started at 5:7. Ask: is this row correct, and how do you know?
quick_checks.look_for: Yes -- both parts doubled (same multiplier). A student who checks by adding ('both went up by 5 and 7') is verifying the right row for a reason that will fail them later.

worked_solution.stem: A flower shop uses 7 daisies for every 4 roses in a bouquet. How many daisies are needed when 32 roses are used?

steps.annotation: Place the given amount under its own quantity. 32 is roses, not daisies.
Find what the roses' ratio number was multiplied by: 32 / 4 = 8.
Carry the SAME multiplier across to the daisies column.
The row reduces back to the original ratio, so the table row is genuine.

faded_example.stem: A snack mix uses 3 cups of nuts for every 8 cups of cereal. How many cups of nuts are needed for 40 cups of cereal?

steps.math: 40 is cereal, and 8 x 5 = 40 -- the multiplier is 5
steps.annotation: The given amount belongs to the cereal column; find what 8 was multiplied by.
Multiply the nuts' ratio number by that same multiplier.
Check: does your pair reduce back to 3:8 when you divide both parts by 5?

sentence_starters: The given number belongs to the ___ column, so the multiplier is ___ / ___ = ___.
I carried the multiplier ___ across the row, so the missing value is ___ x ___ = ___.

skills.name: Write and evaluate an expression to solve a ratio problem
skills.i_do_script: When the numbers get big, the table gets long -- so we compress the strategy into one expression. Popcorn buckets sell in a ratio of large to small of 3:2, and 324 SMALL buckets were sold. The given amount is small buckets, so divide by SMALL's ratio part: 324 / 2 = 162. Then multiply by large's part: 162 x 3 = 486. The whole strategy is one line: (324 / 2) x 3. Divide by the part that matches the given, multiply by the part you want.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the given amount by the wrong ratio part -- sets up (given / other part) x matching part, a reversed setup
canonical_error.example: Large to small is 3:2 and 324 small buckets were sold. Student writes (324 / 3) x 2 = 216 instead of (324 / 2) x 3 = 486
canonical_error.why: The student grabs the ratio numbers in the order they were written instead of matching the given quantity to ITS OWN ratio part. When the ratio is stated in the reverse order of the given, the first number is the wrong one.

redirect_script.stop: Pause -- which ratio number belongs to the amount you were GIVEN?
redirect_script.prompt: Label each ratio number with its unit: 3 = large, 2 = small. You were given SMALL buckets, so divide by small's number. Rewrite your expression with the labels attached.
redirect_script.praise: You matched the given amount to its own ratio part before dividing -- that's the whole setup.

skills.item_template: A two-part item (spec's At-proficiency MP shape): a ratio a:b with a large given amount of the second quantity (triple-digit allowed). Part A: write the expression (given / its part) x other part. Part B: evaluate it. Also MC items on choosing the correct expression.

sample_items.stem: A movie theater sells large and small popcorn buckets in a ratio of 3:2. The theater sold 324 small buckets. Part A: What expression can be used to find the number of large buckets sold? Part B: How many large buckets were sold?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversed setup (324 / 3) x 2 = 216 divides by large's part even though small buckets were given

sample_items.stem: A pizza shop sells cheese and pepperoni pizzas in a ratio of 5:3. The shop sold 120 pepperoni pizzas. Part A: What expression can be used to find the number of cheese pizzas sold? Part B: How many cheese pizzas were sold?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversed setup (120 / 5) x 3 = 72 divides by cheese's part even though pepperoni was given

sample_items.stem: A library's ratio of fiction to nonfiction checkouts is 4:5. There were 85 nonfiction checkouts. Part A: What expression can be used to find the number of fiction checkouts? Part B: How many fiction checkouts were there?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversed setup (85 / 4) x 5 divides by fiction's part; it doesn't even come out whole, which is itself a red flag worth naming

sample_items.stem: The ratio of granola bars to juice boxes at a camp is 2:7. There are 42 juice boxes. Which expression finds the number of granola bars?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (42 / 2) x 7 is the reversed setup; 42 x 7 x 2 multiplies everything in sight; 42 + 7 - 2 reasons additively

vocabulary.definition: A math phrase that shows the strategy in symbols, like (324 / 2) x 3.
A comparison of two amounts in a specific order -- each number belongs to one named quantity.
The value of (given / its ratio part) -- how many times the ratio was scaled up.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S5 (unit pricing and speed) or S6 (comparing ratios) -- the strategy is now portable symbols.
next_steps.if_fail: Go back to S3 and solve the same problems WITH the table visible; then write the expression next to the table so the student sees the two are the same moves.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'Large to small popcorn buckets are sold in a ratio of 3:2. The theater sold 324 small buckets. How many large buckets?'
Before any math: label the ratio numbers. Which number is large buckets and which is small?
Write '3 = large, 2 = small' above the ratio. Circle '324 small' in the problem.
The 324 is SMALL buckets. Which ratio number is its partner -- 3 or 2?
So what division finds the multiplier? Say it with units: '324 small divided by...'
If the student writes 324 / 3, point at their labels: 'Is 3 the small-bucket number? Which number did you circle as small?' Let the labels catch the reversal.
Write the full expression: (324 / 2) x 3. Compute it together: 162, then 486.
The recipe for the expression never changes: divide the given by ITS OWN ratio part, multiply by the part you want. Labels first, math second.

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of boys to girls is 1:2 and there are 10 girls. Which expression finds the number of boys: (10 / 2) x 1 or (10 / 1) x 2? What is the answer?
The ratio of red to blue is 3:4 and you are given 20 BLUE. Fill in the blank: multiplier = 20 / ___.
A stadium sells large and small drinks in a ratio of 4:3. Fans bought 96 small drinks. Write the expression and find how many large drinks were sold.
practice_problems.notes: Watch for (96 / 4) x 3 = 72 -- the reversed setup.

practice_problems.stem: Mateo set up an expression for this problem. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The ratio of large to small buckets is 3:2.
practice_problems.answer: Mateo divided by 3, but 3 is the LARGE buckets' number -- he was given SMALL buckets. Correct setup: (84 / 2) x 3 = 42 x 3 = 126 large buckets.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical reversed-setup error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A bookstore's ratio of hardcover to paperback sales is 2:9. It sold 63 paperbacks. How many hardcovers did it sell?
The ratio of red beads to blue beads is 5:4. Write an equation for the number of red beads r when there are b blue beads.
practice_problems.notes: The general equation is the standard's 'equations' model in its purest form.

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of SMALL to LARGE cups sold is 2:3 -- careful, small is named first this time. The cafe sold 141 large cups. How many small cups did it sell?
practice_problems.notes: Reverse order (spec's 'difficult' move): the given quantity is named SECOND in the ratio.

practice_problems.stem: For 'the ratio of apps to games is 5:4, and there are 140 games,' two students wrote (140 / 4) x 5 and (140 / 5) x 4. Which is correct, what does it equal, and how do you know in ONE sentence?
practice_problems.answer: (140 / 4) x 5 = 175 apps. You divide by 4 because 4 is the ratio part that belongs to games -- the quantity that was given.
practice_problems.notes: Explain-the-contrast stretch: articulating WHY kills the reversed setup.

activities.title: Expression Lineup
materials: Story cards and expression cards (cut apart)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread story cards on the left, expression cards on the right.
2. For each story, partners label the ratio numbers with units OUT LOUD ('6 is tents, 5 is campers... wait, check the order') before touching an expression card.
3. Match, then evaluate one matched pair per partner.
4. Debrief: every wrong card was wrong the same way -- what way?

pairs.left: Large to small is 3:2; 84 small sold. Find large.
Cheese to pepperoni is 5:3; 120 pepperoni sold. Find cheese.
Fiction to nonfiction is 4:5; 85 nonfiction. Find fiction.
Small to large is 2:3; 141 large sold. Find small.

activities.title: The Reversed Setup
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Mateo's work (84 / 3 for a 3:2 ratio with 84 SMALL given).
2. Ask the group to label each number in his expression with a unit. The labels expose the mismatch on their own.
3. Rebuild the expression with labels first: (84 small / 2 small-part) x 3 large-part.
4. Each student writes the one question they should ask themselves before dividing ('Which ratio number belongs to the given amount?').

content.worked_problem: Large to small is 3:2. The theater sold 84 small buckets. Mateo wrote (84 / 3) x 2 = 56.
content.error_step: Mateo divided the given amount by 3 -- the LARGE buckets' ratio part -- even though 84 counts SMALL buckets.
content.why: The division must undo the scaling of the quantity you were GIVEN. Since 84 is small buckets and small's part is 2, the multiplier is 84 / 2 = 42, and large = 42 x 3 = 126.

activities.title: Label-First Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Post a ratio story with a given amount ('Tents to campers is 2:7; there are 63 campers').
2. Round 1: students write ONLY the labeled ratio ('2 = tents, 7 = campers') -- no math allowed. Boards up.
3. Round 2: students write ONLY the division that finds the multiplier (63 / 7). Boards up.
4. Round 3: full expression and answer ((63 / 7) x 2 = 18).
5. Mix in one reverse-order story ('Small to large is 2:3; 141 LARGE sold') and debrief why round 1 matters most on that one.

strategy_links.why: The label-divide-multiply routine hands off cleanly: I do it with labels spoken aloud, we do it with labels written, you do it alone.
Pairing a correct worked expression with a reversed one and asking 'which is right and why' targets the exact failure mode of this skill.
Whiteboard rounds where students show ONLY the setup (before any arithmetic) catch reversed divisions while they're still cheap to fix.

questioning_prompts: Label the ratio numbers with units before you write anything. Which number is the given amount's partner?
Say your expression in words with units: '324 small buckets divided by...' Does the sentence make sense?
What does the number you get after dividing MEAN in the story? (It's the number of ratio groups.)
Your answer is smaller than the given amount. The ratio says large outsells small -- should it be smaller?
If I changed the story to give you LARGE buckets instead, which number in your expression would change?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the given amount by the wrong ratio part -- writes (324 / 3) x 2 when 324 is the SMALL-bucket count in a 3:2 large-to-small ratio.
misconception_redirects.say: Label each ratio number with its unit: 3 = large, 2 = small. You were given SMALL buckets, so divide by small's number. Rewrite your expression with the labels attached.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the given amount to its own ratio part before dividing -- that's the whole setup.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student's division doesn't come out whole (85 / 4) and they push on with a decimal or round it.
misconception_redirects.say: A messy division here is a smoke alarm, not a math problem. Whole-number ratio problems scale evenly -- go back and check which ratio part you divided by.
misconception_redirects.praise: You treated the ugly decimal as a warning and re-checked your setup -- great instinct.

quick_checks.prompt: Ratio of dogs to cats is 4:5; there are 45 cats. Just write the expression -- don't solve it.
quick_checks.look_for: (45 / 5) x 4. Writing (45 / 4) x 5 is the reversed setup; writing 45 x 5 x 4 or 4 x 5 means the student has no setup routine at all.

quick_checks.prompt: In the expression (96 / 3) x 4, what does the 96 / 3 part tell you about the story?
quick_checks.look_for: 'How many ratio groups there are' (32 groups). A student who can't say what the quotient means is executing a memorized shape and will reverse it under pressure.

worked_solution.stem: A movie theater sells large and small popcorn buckets in a ratio of 3:2. The theater sold 324 small buckets. How many large buckets did it sell?

steps.annotation: Label the ratio parts with units and circle what was given. The given amount's partner is 2.
Divide the given by ITS OWN ratio part -- 162 is the number of ratio groups.
Multiply by the part you want. The whole expression is (324 / 2) x 3.
The answer pair reduces back to the original ratio.

faded_example.stem: A pizza shop sells cheese and pepperoni pizzas in a ratio of 5:3. The shop sold 120 pepperoni pizzas. How many cheese pizzas did it sell?

steps.annotation: Label the parts, then divide the given amount by its own ratio part.
Multiply the number of groups by the cheese part.
Write the full expression in one line and check that your pair reduces to 5:3.

sentence_starters: The given amount is ___, and its ratio part is ___, so I divide ___ / ___.
My expression is (___ / ___) x ___ because I divide by the given's part and multiply by the part I want.

skills.name: Solve real-world rate problems, including unit prices and constant speed
skills.i_do_script: Real stores and real trips run on rates. To compare two deals, you can't compare the price tags -- you compare what ONE unit costs. Store A sells 4 pounds of apples for $12, Store B sells 6 pounds for $15. A: 12 / 4 = $3 per pound. B: 15 / 6 = $2.50 per pound. B wins, even though its price tag is bigger. 'Cheaper total' and 'cheaper per pound' are different questions.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares totals instead of unit rates -- picks the smaller total price (or bigger package) as the better deal without dividing
canonical_error.example: Store A: 4 pounds for $12 ($3/lb). Store B: 6 pounds for $15 ($2.50/lb). Student picks Store A 'because $12 is less than $15'
canonical_error.why: The student answers 'which number is smaller?' instead of 'which costs less PER UNIT?' They aren't holding the quantity equal, so the price comparison is meaningless -- the packages are different sizes.

redirect_script.stop: Careful -- those two prices aren't for the same amount.
redirect_script.prompt: Make the packages fair: divide each price by its number of units to find the cost of ONE. Write both unit prices side by side, then compare.
redirect_script.praise: You compared the cost of ONE unit from each -- now the comparison is fair.

skills.item_template: A real-world rate in context (a per b), scaled to a new amount -- plus unit-price comparison items with a data_table of brands/sizes/prices. NR for scaling; MC for better-buy items where one distractor compares totals.

sample_items.stem: A garden center plants 3 flowers for every 2 feet of garden bed. How many flowers are needed for 12 feet of garden bed?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Additive reasoning gives 13 (12 + 1); multiplying the ratio parts gives 6; the multiplier is 12 / 2 = 6, so 3 x 6 = 18

sample_items.stem: Elena makes lemonade using 4 teaspoons of sugar for every 6 lemons. She has 18 lemons. How many teaspoons of sugar does she need?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Multiplier is 18 / 6 = 3, so 4 x 3 = 12; multiplying 4 x 6 = 24 is the partners-multiplied error

sample_items.stem: The table shows two cereal brands. Which brand costs less per ounce?
sample_items.answer: Oat Loops, because it costs $0.25 per ounce and Crunchy Os costs $0.30 per ounce
choices: Oat Loops, because it costs $0.25 per ounce
Crunchy Os, because it costs $0.30 per ounce
Crunchy Os, because $3.60 is less than $4.50
They cost the same per ounce
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice c compares total prices without dividing (the canonical error); choice b computes the unit rates but picks the larger one; choice d guesses without computing

sample_items.stem: Gas costs $3 per gallon. Mr. Lee spends $45 filling his tank. How many gallons did he buy?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Reversed direction -- total given, units unknown; multiplying gives 135, the wrong direction

vocabulary.definition: The cost of exactly ONE unit -- one ounce, one pound, one juice box. Divide the price by the number of units.
The amount for one unit of the other quantity -- 50 miles per hour, 12 pages per minute.
A ratio between two different kinds of units, like dollars and ounces or miles and hours.
The choice with the LOWER unit price -- not necessarily the lower price tag.

next_steps.if_pass: Move to S6 (compare two ratios in a multi-step problem) -- the student is ready for the standard's ceiling.
next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to S2 and rebuild the divide-first move on single rates before comparing two of them.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'Store A: 4 pounds of apples for $12. Store B: 6 pounds for $15. Which store is the better buy?'
A student says Store A, 'because $12 is less than $15.' What's wrong with that comparison?
If your student agrees with the fictional student, ask: 'Would 100 pounds for $20 be a bad deal because $20 is more than $12?' The extreme case breaks the totals habit.
How could we make the two stores fair to compare? What if we knew the price of exactly ONE pound at each?
Write: A: 12 / 4 = $3 per pound. B: 15 / 6 = $2.50 per pound.
Now the packages are the same size -- one pound each. Which store charges less?
So can a store have a HIGHER price tag and still be the better buy? When?
Every 'better buy' and 'faster car' question is the same move: divide to get the per-ONE amount, then compare. Price tags and finish-line totals lie; unit rates don't.

practice_problems.stem: Bananas cost $2 per pound. How much do 4 pounds cost?
A robot vacuum cleans 5 square feet every minute. How many square feet does it clean in 8 minutes?
A bakery uses 5 cups of flour for every 3 dozen cookies. How many cups of flour are needed for 12 dozen cookies?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier 12 / 3 = 4, so 5 x 4 = 20.

practice_problems.stem: Jordan compared two apple deals. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Store A sells 4 pounds of apples for $12.
Store B sells 6 pounds of apples for $15.
Store A is the better buy.
practice_problems.answer: Jordan compared the price tags, but the bags are different sizes. Unit prices: A is 12 / 4 = $3 per pound; B is 15 / 6 = $2.50 per pound. Store B is the better buy.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical totals-comparison error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: The table shows two packs of juice boxes. Which pack is the better buy per box?
practice_problems.answer: The small pack -- $6 / 8 = $0.75 per box, versus $8 / 10 = $0.80 per box
practice_problems.notes: Twist: the BIGGER pack is the worse deal here. Students who assume 'bulk is always cheaper' get caught.

practice_problems.stem: A landscaper plants 6 shrubs for every 4 yards of fence. How many shrubs does she plant along 24 yards of fence?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier 24 / 4 = 6, so 6 x 6 = 36. Watch for 24 (6 x 4).

practice_problems.stem: A store sells 16 ounces of juice for $8. What is the unit price per ounce, and how much would 30 ounces cost at that rate?
practice_problems.notes: The unit rate is a decimal -- allowed by the spec exactly here, when identifying a unit rate.

practice_problems.stem: Invent a shopping situation where the LOWER price tag is the WORSE deal per unit. Give both unit prices to prove it.
practice_problems.answer: Any valid example, e.g. 2 pounds for $8 ($4/lb) versus 5 pounds for $15 ($3/lb): the $8 bag has the lower tag but the higher unit price.
practice_problems.notes: Producing the counterexample shows the student truly separates total price from unit price.

activities.title: Grocery Showdown
materials: 6 index cards, each with a 'product' (name, size, price)
activities.instructions:
1. Make three head-to-head pairs of cards, e.g. '12 oz peanut butter, $3.60' vs '18 oz, $4.50'; '8 juice boxes, $6' vs '10 juice boxes, $8'; '4 lb apples, $12' vs '6 lb apples, $15.'
2. For each pair, partners FIRST predict the better buy by gut, writing it down.
3. Then they compute both unit prices and circle the true winner.
4. Debrief: how many predictions flipped after dividing? Which card design fooled you -- big pack or small price tag?

activities.title: Rate to Unit Rate
activities.instructions:
1. Match each rate story to its unit rate.
2. Say the division out loud before matching ('20 dollars for 4 pounds -- 20 / 4 -- 5 per pound').
3. The two decoys match NOTHING -- if you use one, re-check your division.
4. Debrief: which stories gave the units in the reverse order of the question?

activities.title: The Price-Tag Trap
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Jordan's work (picked the $12 bag over the $15 bag without dividing).
2. Ask: what question did Jordan actually answer? ('Which tag is smaller?') What question did the problem ask?
3. Have the group compute both unit prices and write the fair comparison.
4. Each student finishes the sentence: 'A price tag alone can't tell you the better buy because ___.'

content.worked_problem: Store A: 4 lb for $12. Store B: 6 lb for $15. Jordan wrote: $12 < $15, so Store A is the better buy.
content.error_step: Jordan compared the two totals even though the bags hold different amounts.
content.why: A fair comparison needs equal quantities. Dividing gives the price of ONE pound at each store ($3 vs $2.50), and the bigger tag turns out to be the better deal.

strategy_links.why: Number Talks on quick unit prices ($6 for 8 boxes, $45 for 5 tickets) build the divide-first reflex this skill runs on.
Thinking aloud 'these packages are different sizes, so I can't compare tags yet' models the fairness check students skip.
Predict-then-verify better-buy problems spark real disagreement -- Think-Pair-Share turns that disagreement into the reason for unit rates.

questioning_prompts: Are those two prices for the same amount? If not, what would make the comparison fair?
What does ONE ounce cost at each brand? What does ONE hour of driving cover?
Can the bigger package ever be the worse deal? How would you catch it?
You found $0.25 and $0.30 -- which one wins, and what are the units on those numbers?
The problem gives dollars first and ounces second. Which one do you divide BY to get price per ounce?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the smaller total price (or the bigger package) as the better buy without computing unit prices.
misconception_redirects.say: Make the packages fair: divide each price by its number of units to find the cost of ONE. Write both unit prices side by side, then compare.
misconception_redirects.praise: You compared the cost of ONE unit from each -- now the comparison is fair.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides in the wrong order (12 / 3.60 or 5 / 65) and reports a unit rate that doesn't match its units.
misconception_redirects.say: Say the units of your answer out loud: dollars PER ounce means dollars divided by ounces. Write the units into the division before the numbers.
misconception_redirects.praise: You let the units set up the division -- the numbers just followed.

quick_checks.prompt: 12 ounces for $3.60 or 18 ounces for $4.50 -- which is the better buy? You have 30 seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: 18 oz at $0.25/oz beats $0.30/oz. Picking the 12 oz 'because $3.60 is less' is the totals error; picking 18 oz 'because bigger is always cheaper' is a guess -- ask for the two unit prices.

quick_checks.prompt: A car goes 120 miles in 3 hours. At the same speed, how far in 5 hours?
quick_checks.look_for: 200 miles via 40 mph. An answer of 600 (120 x 5) means the student used the 3-hour total as a per-hour rate -- send them back to S2's 'for one or for several?' check.

worked_solution.stem: Store A sells 4 pounds of apples for $12. Store B sells 6 pounds for $15. Which store is the better buy?

steps.annotation: The bags are different sizes, so the price tags can't be compared directly.
Divide each price by ITS number of pounds to get the cost of one pound.
Same move for Store B. Now both numbers describe the same amount: one pound.
The store with the LOWER unit price is the better buy -- even though its price tag is bigger.

faded_example.stem: Elena makes lemonade using 4 teaspoons of sugar for every 6 lemons. She has 18 lemons. How many teaspoons of sugar does she need?

steps.math: 18 lemons, and 6 x 3 = 18 -- the multiplier is 3
steps.annotation: The given amount is lemons; find what 6 was multiplied by.
Multiply the sugar's ratio part by the same multiplier.
Check: does your pair of sugar and lemons reduce back to 4:6?

sentence_starters: ___ is the better buy because its unit price ___ is less than ___.

skills.name: Compare two ratios by scaling each to a common quantity
skills.i_do_script: Now we hold two ratios side by side. A grocery store sold red and green apples: in September, 5 red for every 4 green; in October, 8 red for every 4 green. Each month it sold 52 green apples. You can't just say '8 minus 5 is 3 more' -- those are ratio parts, not real apples. Scale BOTH months to 52 green (multiplier 52 / 4 = 13): September is 5 x 13 = 65 red, October is 8 x 13 = 104 red. The real difference is 39 apples.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares the ratio numbers directly -- subtracts the two first-quantity parts and reports that as the real-world difference without scaling
canonical_error.example: September 5:4, October 8:4, with 52 green apples each month. Student answers 8 - 5 = 3 more red apples instead of scaling by 13 to get 104 - 65 = 39
canonical_error.why: The student treats the ratio numbers as actual counts. A ratio part is a per-group amount; it only becomes a real count after multiplying by the number of groups (52 / 4 = 13 of them).

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- are those real apples, or parts of a ratio?
redirect_script.prompt: Find the multiplier first: how many ratio groups fit in the real amount? Scale EACH ratio up to the real amount, write both real counts, and only then subtract.
redirect_script.praise: You scaled both ratios to the real amount before comparing -- that's the whole skill.

skills.item_template: Two ratios sharing a common second quantity (or scalable to one), plus a real amount of that quantity. Student scales both ratios and answers a 'how many more' or 'which is greater per unit' question. NR (DOK 3); one MC variant on choosing the correct comparison reasoning.

sample_items.stem: A grocery store sold red and green apples in two months. September: for every 5 red apples, 4 green apples. October: for every 8 red apples, 4 green apples. Each month the store sold 52 green apples. How many more red apples were sold in October than in September?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Direct comparison gives 3 (8 - 5) without scaling; the multiplier is 52 / 4 = 13, so 104 - 65 = 39

sample_items.stem: A cookie shop tracks chocolate and vanilla cookie sales. Week 1: 3 chocolate for every 10 vanilla. Week 2: 7 chocolate for every 10 vanilla. Each week the shop sold 40 vanilla cookies. How many more chocolate cookies were sold in Week 2 than in Week 1?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Direct comparison gives 4 (7 - 3) without scaling; the multiplier is 40 / 10 = 4, so 28 - 12 = 16

sample_items.stem: Two classes recycle. Class A collects 4 cans for every 9 bottles. Class B collects 7 cans for every 9 bottles. Each class collected 63 bottles. How many more cans did Class B collect than Class A?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Direct comparison gives 3 (7 - 4) without scaling; the multiplier is 63 / 9 = 7, so 49 - 28 = 21

sample_items.stem: Recipe A uses 2 cups of sugar for every 3 batches of muffins. Recipe B uses 3 cups of sugar for every 5 batches. Which recipe uses more sugar per batch?
sample_items.answer: Recipe A, because 2/3 of a cup per batch is more than 3/5 of a cup per batch
choices: Recipe A, because 2/3 of a cup per batch is more than 3/5 of a cup per batch
Recipe B, because 3 cups is more than 2 cups
Recipe B, because 5 batches is more than 3 batches
They use the same amount per batch
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choices b and c compare single ratio numbers directly (the canonical error); choice d guesses without finding either per-batch amount

vocabulary.definition: The matching amount you scale both ratios to so the comparison is fair -- like 52 green apples in both months.
A per-group comparison. Its numbers are not real counts until you multiply by the number of groups.
How many ratio groups fit in the real amount -- 52 green apples / 4 per group = 13 groups.

next_steps.if_pass: This student is ready for 7.RP.2 (proportional relationships) -- constant of proportionality is the unit rate they've been using.
next_steps.if_fail: Have them solve each month as its OWN S3-style problem first, writing both real counts, then hand back the comparison question.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'September: 5 red for every 4 green. October: 8 red for every 4 green. Each month, 52 green apples were sold. How many more red in October than September?'
A student answers '3 more, because 8 - 5 = 3.' Are 8 and 5 real apple counts? What are they?
If your student defends the 3, ask: 'September sold 52 green apples. Does the ratio 5:4 say the store only sold 5 red apples ALL month?' The absurdity opens the door.
Both months sold 52 green apples, and each ratio group has 4 green. How many ratio groups is that?
Write: 52 / 4 = 13 groups. September: 5 x 13 = 65 red. October: 8 x 13 = 104 red.
NOW how many more red apples in October? And why is 39 exactly 13 times the '3' from before?
The ratio difference (3 per group) was real -- but it happens in EVERY one of the 13 groups. Scale first, compare second.
Your turn: Week 1 is 3 chocolate per 10 vanilla, Week 2 is 7 per 10, and each week sold 40 vanilla. How many more chocolate in Week 2?

practice_problems.stem: Which is the higher price per pound: $10 for 2 pounds or $12 for 3 pounds?
practice_problems.answer: $10 for 2 pounds -- $5 per pound versus $4 per pound

practice_problems.stem: Scale both ratios so the second number is 12: 2:3 and 3:4.

A bookstore sold hardcovers and paperbacks. May: 3 hardcovers for every 11 paperbacks. June: 6 hardcovers for every 11 paperbacks. Each month it sold 44 paperbacks. How many more hardcovers did it sell in June than in May?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier 44 / 11 = 4: June 24, May 12. Direct comparison gives 3 -- the canonical error.

practice_problems.stem: Sam compared two weeks of library loans. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Each week the library loaned 36 nonfiction books.
7 - 4 = 3, so 3 more fiction books in Week 2.
practice_problems.answer: Sam subtracted ratio parts, not real books. The multiplier is 36 / 9 = 4. Week 1: 4 x 4 = 16 fiction. Week 2: 7 x 4 = 28 fiction. The real difference is 28 - 16 = 12 books.
practice_problems.notes: Direct bait for the canonical compare-the-parts error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: Hose A fills 5 gallons every 2 minutes. Hose B fills 7 gallons every 3 minutes. In 12 minutes, how much water does each hose pump, and which pumps more?
practice_problems.answer: Hose A pumps 30 gallons (12 / 2 = 6 groups, 5 x 6). Hose B pumps 28 gallons (12 / 3 = 4 groups, 7 x 4). Hose A pumps more.
practice_problems.notes: Different second quantities -- students must scale each to 12 minutes separately.

practice_problems.stem: Class A gets 3 pizzas for every 8 students. Class B gets 5 pizzas for every 8 students. Each class has 24 students. How many more pizzas does Class B get?
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier 24 / 8 = 3: B gets 15, A gets 9.

practice_problems.stem: Store A gives 2 free stickers for every 5 purchases. Store B gives 2 free stickers for every 4 purchases. Ari makes 20 purchases at EACH store. How many stickers does each store give, and which gives more?
practice_problems.answer: Store A: 20 / 5 = 4 groups, 8 stickers. Store B: 20 / 4 = 5 groups, 10 stickers. Store B gives 2 more.
practice_problems.notes: Same first parts (2 and 2) -- the comparison lives entirely in the second quantity, reversing the usual setup.

practice_problems.stem: Create two different red:blue ratios that both use 24 blue when scaled, where one gives exactly 6 more red than the other. Show the scaling for both.
practice_problems.answer: Any valid pair, e.g. 3:8 and 5:8 -- multiplier 24 / 8 = 3, giving 9 red and 15 red, a difference of 6.
practice_problems.notes: Working backward from the difference shows full control of the scale-then-compare structure.

activities.title: 3 More... or 39 More?
materials: One printed problem card per group
activities.instructions:
1. Show Sam's work (7 - 4 = 3 more fiction books) next to the real question.
2. Ask: what ARE the 7 and the 4? Have the group draw one 'week' as ratio groups -- 4 groups of (7 fiction, 9 nonfiction) versus 4 groups of (4 fiction, 9 nonfiction).
3. Count real books in each drawing and find the true difference (12).
4. Debrief: why did the wrong answer (3) turn out to be exactly the right answer divided by the number of groups?

content.worked_problem: Week 1: 4 fiction per 9 nonfiction. Week 2: 7 fiction per 9 nonfiction. 36 nonfiction each week. Sam wrote: 7 - 4 = 3 more fiction.
content.error_step: Sam subtracted the ratio parts as if they were real book counts.
content.why: Each ratio part happens once per GROUP, and there are 36 / 9 = 4 groups. The per-group difference of 3 happens 4 times: the real difference is 12.

activities.title: Which Deal Wins?
activities.instructions:
1. Post a comparison card, e.g. 'Team A scores 3 goals every 2 games; Team B scores 4 goals every 3 games. Both play 12 games.'
2. Partner 1 scales Team A, Partner 2 scales Team B -- each on their own board (A: 18 goals, B: 16 goals).
3. Boards together: write the comparison sentence ('A scores 2 more').
4. Swap roles each round. A pair scores only if BOTH boards and the sentence are right.
5. Last round: a card where the tempting direct comparison picks the WRONG winner -- discuss.

activities.title: Fair or Unfair Comparison?
activities.instructions:
1. Lay out headers 'Fair comparison' and 'Unfair -- not the same quantity yet.'
2. Partners sort each comparison statement and defend each placement in one sentence.
3. For every 'unfair' card, say what would make it fair (scale to a common amount).
4. Debrief: what did every unfair card have in common?

categories: Unfair -- not the same quantity yet

Both hoses measured over the same 12 minutes
5 red per 4 green vs 8 red per 4 green -- so 3 more red were sold
cards.category: Unfair -- not the same quantity yet

cards.category: Unfair -- not the same quantity yet
