strategy_links.why: The 3-vs-39 surprise creates genuine disagreement -- structured pair talk turns the argument into the reason for scaling first.
Setting a correct scaled solution beside the direct-subtraction one and asking what each '3' means targets this skill's exact failure.
The compare-the-parts error is stable and predictable; analyzing it explicitly is faster than hoping more practice dissolves it.

questioning_prompts: Are the numbers you're comparing real counts, or ratio parts? How do you know?
How many ratio groups fit in the real amount? Show the division.
Both ratios mention 4 green apples. Does that mean the months are already fair to compare? Why?
Your per-group difference is 3 and there are 13 groups. What's the real difference, and why?
The two hoses run for different times in their ratios. What common time would make them fair to compare?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student subtracts the two ratio parts directly (8 - 5 = 3) and reports it as the real-world difference.
misconception_redirects.say: Find the multiplier first: how many ratio groups fit in the real amount? Scale EACH ratio up to the real amount, write both real counts, and only then subtract.
misconception_redirects.praise: You scaled both ratios to the real amount before comparing -- that's the whole skill.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student scales one ratio but compares it to the other ratio's raw part (compares 104 to 8).
misconception_redirects.say: Every number in your final comparison must be a REAL count. Point to each number and say what it counts -- if one of them is still a ratio part, scale it before comparing.
misconception_redirects.praise: Both of your numbers are real counts now, so the subtraction actually means something.

quick_checks.prompt: Ratios 2:5 and 4:5, with 20 of the second quantity in each. What's the real difference in the first quantity?
quick_checks.look_for: Multiplier 4, counts 8 and 16, difference 8. An answer of 2 (4 - 2) is the compare-the-parts error -- ask what the 2 counts.

quick_checks.prompt: Two ratios have second parts 2 and 3. What common amount could you scale both to for a fair comparison?
quick_checks.look_for: 6 (or any common multiple, or 'per 1'). Not knowing where 6 comes from means the student can't yet set up unlike-denominator comparisons -- pre-teach with the hoses problem.

worked_solution.stem: September: 5 red apples for every 4 green. October: 8 red for every 4 green. Each month, 52 green apples were sold. How many more red apples were sold in October than in September?

steps.annotation: Both ratios have 4 green per group, and 52 real green apples were sold -- so each month has 13 ratio groups.
Scale September's red part by the number of groups to get a REAL count.
Same multiplier for October -- the green apples matched, so the groups match.
Only now subtract: both numbers are real apple counts. (Notice 39 = 3 x 13 -- the per-group gap happened in all 13 groups.)

faded_example.stem: Week 1: 3 chocolate cookies for every 10 vanilla. Week 2: 7 chocolate for every 10 vanilla. Each week, 40 vanilla cookies were sold. How many more chocolate cookies were sold in Week 2?

steps.annotation: Each week has 4 ratio groups, since 40 real vanilla at 10 per group.
Scale Week 1's chocolate part to a real count.
Scale Week 2's chocolate part with the same multiplier.
Subtract the two REAL counts to find how many more.

sentence_starters: The real amount is ___, so there are ___ / ___ = ___ ratio groups.
After scaling, the real counts are ___ and ___, so the difference is ___.

foundation.label: Foundation
foundation.description: Tier III -- 2+ grade levels below. If a student can't access Looking Back, start here.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Prerequisite skills -- fix these first if a student can't access grade-level work

looking_forward.label: Looking Forward
looking_forward.description: Extension skills -- for students ready to push ahead

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (use a table of equivalent ratios) -- it sits at the heart of the standard. If the student passes, check S4 (equations) and S5 (unit rates and unit pricing), then S6 (comparing ratios) for students ready to push. If S3 fails, drop back to S1 (scale a ratio) and S2 (use a rate) to find whether the gap is the scaling move itself or the per-one idea. A student who can't attempt S1 needs the Foundation skills (facts and ratio writing).
